text: Good morning and welcome to Procter & Gamble's quarter-end conference call.
Today's event is being recorded for replay.
This discussion will include a number of forward-looking statements.
If you will refer to P&G's most recent 10K, 10Q, and 8K reports, you will see a discussion
of factors that could cause the company's actual results to differ materially from these
projections. As required by Regulation G, Procter & Gamble needs to make you aware that during the
discussion, the company will make a number of references to non-GAAP and other financial
measures. Procter & Gamble believes these measures provide investors with useful
perspective on underlying business trends and has posted on its investor relations website,
www.pginvestor.com, a full reconciliation of non-GAAP financial measures.
Now I will turn the call over to P&G's Chief Financial Officer, Andre Schulten.
Good morning everyone. Joining me on the call today are Kerry Cohn and John Chevalier,
our Senior Vice Presidents of Investor Relations. I'll start with an overview of
results for the first quarter of fiscal 27 and discuss the progress we are making against
our near-term priorities and longer-term transformation efforts. I'll close with
guidance for fiscal 27 and then we will take your questions.
We are pleased with the continued acceleration in top line results in our first quarter of fiscal
year 27. Bottom line results reflect the strength of the top line progress and productivity
to offset the higher costs from raw materials, energy, and increasing freight costs, primarily
in North America. We expect these headwinds to increase in the next few quarters. Taken
together, we remain on track to deliver within our guidance ranges for the fiscal year.
Before I share the detailed results, you may have noticed in the press release beginning
this fiscal year, we will report sales growth to one decimal place at both the company
and the sector level. And with that, organic sales increased 4.0% versus the prior year.
We see sequential progress from our targeted interventions at the category and country level.
By delivering superiority, we are winning with consumers and driving improved consumption
semester over semester into this first quarter. Volume increased 2.4 points,
pricing was up 0.4 points, and mix was up over a point for the quarter. A solid balance
across top line drivers and with a majority of growth driven by volume. We delivered broad-based
growth across the business with each of our 10 product categories growing organic sales.
Fabric care, home care, baby care, hair care, skin and personal care, and grooming grew
mid-singles. Family care, feminine care, oral care, and personal health care each grew
low single digits. Growth was also broad-based geographically with each of our six regions
growing organic sales. Focus markets were up 4%. Organic sales in North America grew 3%
and the U.S. market also was up 3%. In North America, volume was up 3 points driven by
continued improvement in consumption across categories. We now have over 70% of our top
U.S. customers holding or growing share, up from less than 10% in the first half of fiscal 26
and 50% in the second half of last fiscal year. Europe region was up 4% with all key markets
growing that by high single-digit growth in the U.K. Greater China organic sales grew 8%
continued strong growth in what remains a challenging consumer environment. Pampers and
SK2 led the growth with SK2 up 12% and Pampers up close to 50% benefiting from near-term
competitive dynamics. Enterprise markets in aggregate grew 5% for the quarter. Note the
makeup of enterprise markets has changed this fiscal year, now made up of Latin America,
Asia Pacific enterprise, and our newly combined IMETA or India, Middle East, Turkey, and Africa
region. This change emphasizes the growth opportunity across emerging markets and creates
a one Europe region structure to simplify the Europe operating framework. Latin America organic
sales grew 4% led by Mexico up double digits and Brazil up low single digits. Organic sales in
the IMETA region grew 8%. APEC enterprise was up 2%, still impacted by our portfolio restructuring
impacts. Global aggregate market share is flat versus prior year across all time periods.
29 of our top 50 category country combinations held or grew share fiscal year to date
up from 25 in the second half of last fiscal year. Also a reflection of the progress being
made across the portfolio. On the bottom line, core earnings per share were $2,
up one point versus prior year. On a currency neutral basis, core EPS was in line versus
prior year. Core growth margin was down 150 basis points and core operating margin was down 80
basis points versus prior year. Strong productivity improvement of 250 basis points was offset
by commodity and freight costs in addition to demand creation investments.
Currency neutral core operating margin was down 90 basis points. Pre-cash for productivity was
93%. We returned $3.9 billion of cash to share owners in this quarter, $2.6 billion in dividends
and $1.3 billion in share repurchase. In summary, this was a strong start to the year.
Positive sales and share trends across markets consistent with the semester to semester progress
we expected behind the interventions being executed across categories, countries, and customers.
As we move forward, the fundamental elements of our strategy remain unchanged. We are in the
right categories to deliver against our growth goals. These categories are our core competency.
We know how to grow these categories and win with superior innovation, better execution,
and clear communication. We know how to create value in these categories and we have a proven
track record to fund growth via productivity. We have an organization focused on the growth
of consumers and winning with our retail partners. What we are changing is nearly every part of our
execution framework to identify superiority gaps even faster and respond quickly to changes
needed to product, package, communication, retail execution, or value to ignite user growth
of our brands. The adjustments we have made are starting to take hold. Let me share a few
examples. U.S. Pantene Abundant and Strong started with a deep insight and consumer connection.
More than 50% of women will experience noticeable hair loss in their lifetime. In the United
States alone, female pattern hair loss affects approximately 30 million individuals.
Pantene's Abundant and Strong technology grew from research linking scalp oxidative stress
to poor scalp conditions and hair quality. In the United States alone, female pattern hair loss
and hair quality. This led to the development of Pantene's Abundant and Strong collection with a
pro-vitamin complex, proprietary formulation. Consumers are delighted with improvement in hair
strength and less shedding with delightful fragrance and a tingling sensorial experience
in the shower. Pantene is delivering mid-single digit sales growth in the U.S.
and is growing share. Pampus Prestige has been a significant growth driver of our China
baby care business with mid-teen growth consistently over the past eight quarters.
We took the same consumer insight and brought the very best diaper available to the U.S.
with the Amora launch in the second half of last fiscal year. Amora is our most advanced
and premium diaper combining proprietary skin health technologies and premium materials for
superior protection and cashmere-like skin comfort. Built on an engaging social first
brand building model and inspired by insights that fewer babies in each household means
parents spend more per baby. Amora has been one of the most successful launches across multiple
retailers contributing to Pampus share growth and projected to exceed 100 million dollars
in sales in year one. In the Gulf cluster UAE, Oman, Qatar, Kuwait, and Buran,
the percentage of sales growing household penetration increased fourfold from 15 percent
in fiscal 25 to over 60 percent in fiscal 26 despite the market volatility. Fairy Dish
delivered double-digit growth in fiscal 26 into the first quarter of fiscal 27 after the team
transformed how consumers engaged with Fairy. They created a consumer-led user-generated
content campaign that brought to life the toughest dishwashing moments consumers faced
generating a record-breaking engagement at 20 times our branded content benchmark.
As a result, Fairy reclaimed its position as the market's leading equity brand
and grew the category by four points and P&G's share by two points. The other examples we've
discussed recently also continue to deliver strong results including U.S. Tide Boosted
and EVO, Mexico Fabric Enhancers, Brazil Haircare, and U.S. Personal Care. While we
continue to execute our plans in the near term to return to sustainable growth,
we're also making progress on a long-term reinvention of P&G capabilities to become
what we call the CPG company of the future. We are adapting our capabilities, systems,
and organization structure to take advantage of significant growth opportunities we see across
our markets and overcome the external landscape changes impacting our industry.
We are leveraging the deepest and most extensive consumer understanding in the industry driven by
learning and data for millions of consumers. This understanding leads to insights and signals
that drive faster and better innovations grounded in industry-leading research, development,
modeling, and testing capabilities. We have the strongest ability to authentically engage
consumers building on our trusted and loved brands. We have widespread access to consumer
paths to purchase via strong retailer partnerships and our supply chain is a differentiator where a
resilient agile supply chain is critical to respond to global volatility and cost pressures.
We have the highest output productivity program in the industry. Winning with consumers is what
matters and the companies that can best respond to the changing environment and leverage the
fast-evolving technologies and capabilities to follow the consumer closely are the ones that
will truly lead the industry. We intend this to be P&G. Moving to guidance, as you saw in our
press release this morning, we are maintaining our fiscal 27 guidance ranges across organic
sales, core EPS, and free cash flow productivity. We expect the environment around us to remain
volatile and challenging from cost to currencies to consumer, competitor, retailer, and geopolitical
dynamics. Our all-in-gap outlook now includes the Thorn business which closed in early October.
We continue to expect sales growth of 1 to 3 percent. We started the year above this range
but we expect growth to be volatile quarter to quarter due to base periods dynamics.
Also we'll be closely watching consumer demand as high fuel and energy costs persist into the
fall and winter. As a reminder, our top line guidance includes roughly 30 to 50 basis points
headwinds from product and market exits that are part of our restructuring work.
Our bottom line guidance is for core EPS growth of 0 to 3 percent versus prior year and this
equates to a range of 6.89 to $7.11 per share. This outlook includes a cost headwind of
approximately $1.4 billion after tax driven by higher raw material, energy, and transportation
costs and other premiums resulting primarily from the conflict in the Middle East.
This estimate assumes an effective Brent crude oil price of $100 a barrel.
Due to the duration of higher oil prices we now expect materially higher cost headwinds in Q2
and the second half of fiscal 27. We expect the foreign exchange headwind of approximately
$50 million after tax. We also expect approximately $300 million of higher net
interest expense after tax, around $150 million higher due to the debt issuance related to
recent M&A activity. These impacts start in the second quarter. Finally we still forecast
$150 million after tax of lower non-operating income. We now expect that our core effective
tax rate will be in the range of 20 to 21 percent. Combined input costs, foreign exchange,
items below the operating line will be a roughly $1.9 billion after tax headwind of earnings
in fiscal 27 or 79 cents per share, 11 percent of fiscal 26 core EPS versus the 56 cents per
share or 8 percent impact shared in July earnings call. We expect capital spending will be between
4.5 to 5.5 percent of sales. We are forecasting free cash flow productivity at 85 percent to 90
percent for the year. We expect to pay over $10 billion in dividends and to repurchase
approximately $5 billion of common stock. Combined a plan to return $15 billion of cash to
share owners in fiscal 27. The guidance range reflects the continued acceleration toward our
long-term algorithm. It is a balanced outlook between top line and bottom line despite
significant cost pressures and reflecting current market realities for consumer demand.
We will maintain strong investment in the business balanced by a strong productivity program
with an intent to improve results semester by semester and year by year.
This outlook is based on current market growth rate estimates, commodity prices,
and foreign exchange rates. Significant additional currency weakness, commodity cost
increases, geopolitical disruptions, tariffs, major supply chain disruptions,
or store closures are not anticipated within the guidance range. In summary,
challenging markets like the ones we compete in today are an opportunity for P&G to lead.
We have the brands, the capability, and most importantly the people required to win.
We are confident in the short-term progress we are making behind deliberate plans to drive user
growth of our brands and execution of excellence across each category and country combination.
It won't be a straight line, especially quarter to quarter, and volatility will remain
a near to midterm reality, but we are building momentum with consumers and customers
and we are excited about the long-term opportunities ahead. With that, we'll be happy
to take your questions. If you have a question, please press star followed by one on your phone.
If your question has been answered or you would like to withdraw your question,
press star followed by two. Your first question comes from the line of Lauren Lieberman
of Barclays. Please go ahead. Great, thanks so much. Good morning. We had to go back a ways
in our model to find the last time that P&G posted volumes up more than 2% and organic at 4%.
When we found that time, which was back in I think 22, optically margins are up a lot
more this time around. I was just curious if you could talk about if that's something
specific to the quarter, mixed dynamic, comp dynamics, or if something has changed
structurally so that you're going to see much greater operating leverage at this level of
volume growth. Thanks. Good morning, Lauren. Thanks for the question. I think it's a combination
of quarter specifics and structurals. Let me start with the structurals maybe.
When we see growth around 4% and volume growth at or above 2%, we've always seen leverage.
I think that leverage structurally is increasing. Number one, on the cost of good
side, the level of productivity we're generating is increasing. The amount of automation and
digitization is helping us as we talked for many times as we execute supply chain 3.0.
There's operating leverage on the cost side. The restructuring program, including the 15%
headcount reduction in manufacturing headcount is starting to impact the quarter this fiscal
year. Recall we started the execution last fiscal year first semester, so we're starting
to get impact flowing through the P&L, and that is helping our SG&A leverage.
The third structural component, as we transform our brand building efforts
to include the revised consumer path to purchase and drive engagement at every one of those
touch points, we remain fully invested in the business, but we find ways to make that spending
work harder for us. That's driving top line growth at flat spending, and that is giving the
third structural element of the leverage. I think what is more specific to the quarter
is the fact that we've only seen partial flow through of the commodity impact in the first
quarter. Again, the oil price and petrol complex keeps increasing. So we've outlook at $100 a barrel,
$1.4 billion of after-tax impact. That's 8% for the year of earnings headwind. In quarter
one, we only saw 5% headwind year over year, so that's a little bit of a one-timer that will be
correcting itself as we get towards the ongoing oil price impact through the P&L.
For sure, if oil stays at the level that we saw this morning, north of 110,
that will continue to be an increasing headwind for the year.
The last point I'll give you is we had the second part of the IEPA tariff refund
in quarter one of about $90 million. Those are the two ones that are more
specific to the quarter. I think most encouraging for us are the first three.
We truly drive leverage because we're improving the structural leverage within the P&L.
Your next question will come from the line of Steve Powers of Deutsche Bank. Please go ahead.
Great. Good morning. Thank you very much. Andre, obviously a very strong start to the year.
I wanted to ask around the sustainability of the momentum that we've seen start to emerge
from two perspectives. One is very, very, very tactically in the short term.
As we think about this first semester in the December quarter, were there any shipment timing,
competitive factors, or other dynamics that may have materially flattered one Q at the expense
of two Q? In your mind, just want to get underneath that if I could.
And then stepping back more generally, as you look at the underlying performance
across your 10 categories, I think you said growth across all 10, where do you feel
sustainable momentum is maybe best established versus where you feel there is still more work
to do within those categories? Thank you. Morning, Steve. In summary, what I tell you,
Q1 was a great start. Every region growing, every category growing, and most encouragingly,
if we look at the last few weeks, share is trending up consistently. So that gives me
confidence. I'd still tell you we expect half one to be at about 3% organic sales growth.
That's what we want to deliver, that sequential acceleration semester by semester.
You recall half one of last year, one, half two, two. And we think the right estimate
and the right approach for cadence here is 3% in the first half, and then acceleration into
the second half. As you know, there's always a little bit of wobble between merge events
or when they ship. That's been a little bit of an effect that we saw in Europe, for example.
And so there might be a point shifting from one quarter to the other, but I think the
overarching headline that I want you to take away is 3% for half one and slight acceleration
in half two, which means consistent value and volume share growth throughout the next quarters.
I'm excited, quite frankly, about the progress we're making across each of the categories.
You look at fabric and home care growing strongly. With North America now growing at 5%
in fabric care, we're growing across laundry and we're growing across fabric enhancers,
and there's tons of runway. Baby care consistently growing at a global level.
Even if you exclude the China acceleration, we have very strong results in baby.
Sampia doing great, adult incontinence improving. Beauty care at 5%, very strong,
and across all three segments within beauty care. So I could continue,
but basically you're getting the point. Every category is showing great progress and momentum.
I'll tell you, we're about 60% down the path of fixing each category-country combination.
We're running at 29 out of 50 top category-country combinations growing or holding share.
We need to conquer the rest, and that's the task ahead. I'll tell you,
our beauty team isn't content with 5% of growth. There's way more opportunity in that
space that we need to capture. Family care is not yet back to share growth.
The interventions we are making across price point corrections in the club channel,
the launch of Charmin and Bounty Essentials, all of those are pushing momentum in the right
direction, but we haven't yet seen the share turn. Our healthcare business has been impacted
by a slow cold cough season over the last two years. We've now seen in the most recent couple
of weeks an acceleration. If that holds, there's more growth to be had there.
Don't get too excited. I come back to where I started. 3% in the front half, hopefully a bit
of acceleration in the back half, consistent share growth quarter over quarter. Your next
question will come from the line of Daryl Messinian of Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.
Hey, good morning. So, Andre, you're expecting a pronounced level of commodity pressure this
fiscal year of $1.4 billion, and up another $400 million versus last quarter. Unfortunately,
that's also looking more sustainable than we hoped originally after the run-up earlier this
year. So just in light of how severe the commodity backdrop looks, how do you think
about pricing as an offsetting lever to that cost pressure? And the context of the question is,
still seemingly difficult industry backdrop in theory with a weak developed market consumer,
promotional competitive environment, even some retailer pushback. So just how do you weigh
all those competing forces as you think about pricing in the remainder of the year,
and also the internal progress that you're making from a top line perspective that you
just mentioned in response to Steve's question? Thanks. Good morning, Daryl.
Yeah, I think that's an important place to pause for a moment. Obviously, $1.4 billion,
8% headwind is significant. And again, if we see the most recent development, this
might increase for the year. We will deal with this the same way we always do. And I do feel that
the team is well equipped to handle even the higher level of cost pressure. But it will take
three things. It will take record productivity levels, which we have identified. The project
list is complete and sufficient, and it's being executed across every one of our businesses. So I
feel very good about a sustained record level of productivity output that will help us overcome
a good portion of this cost pressure while we maintain investment in the business.
The second component is pricing with innovation. And honestly, I think the momentum we are starting
to generate gives us confidence to price with innovation because we are getting the
balance between pricing and product improvements, package improvements, claims, communication,
and retail execution right. But it's also a very fragile balance that we want to make sure we
don't compromise on. So we will price, and we will price with innovation, not jeopardizing
the top line momentum. The third component here is time. We will take the right amount of time
to recover the dollar impact of the commodity hurt. And time will be largely driven by what
we described in the second point, making sure we maintain the right balance of price, product,
package, communication, and in-store execution. We have worked, the team has worked so hard
over the last nine months, category by category, customer by customer, country by country,
to improve this balance. So I think we're probably closer to this dynamic than we've
been in a long time. I feel good about the plans that I see. The last point I leave you with
is at this level of commodity pressure, not a projection, just the fact, the industry generally
is pricing up because there is no way to recover this level of commodity pressure
without pricing. That's a fact of the past. It doesn't have to hold true for the future.
So I can just only give you my perspective on the three elements we're going to work on.
Your next question will come from the line of Robert Oddenstein of Evercore ISI. Please go ahead.
Great. And congratulations on the strong start. You know, from everything we're seeing,
clearly a lot of the US categories are improving. You're regaining share. But as you
note, it's a very dynamic environment. So I was wondering if you could talk a little bit
about what you're seeing or expecting in terms of competitor reactions, and then also,
how are you dealing with ongoing affordability issues in terms of dealing with competitors,
as well as maintaining the market share momentum? Thank you.
Thanks for the question, Robert. I think the competitive environment has been
pierced over the last few quarters. And I think that has led us to make adjustments
where we needed to make adjustments. We've talked about our baby care business, where we
needed to get value competitive with a new competitive reality. And I think we've done that
and I feel very good about being balanced. I think we got to a point where we reacted to be
competitive on those hygiene factors, I would call them, and then add superiority in terms
of product performance, communication, better retail execution to drive category growth,
and our growth within that. So I still see the same formula playing out.
Growth going forward is not about taking share. Growth going forward is about growing our
categories. And I'm encouraged to see that in North America, the category is now approaching
3% value growth. In many places, innovation that we're launching with pricing is driving
true category growth. You heard our examples in the prepared remarks on user growth, for example,
in the Middle East. That topic of consistent user growth or penetration growth in our categories
is relevant and being pushed around the world. So I view the competitive dynamic as
unchanged and, yes, intense. I view our role within that as growing categories with innovation,
better offerings for consumers. Affordability within that is that careful balance that we
were describing in every pricing decision. And I think also here we are executing what we have
designed for. We have a portfolio of brands that spans across different value tiers.
And we have a portfolio of pack sizes and executions within each brand
that go from very affordable value offering to high pack size premium offerings,
depending on the cohort, depending on the channel. And I think we're continuously getting sharper in
the execution. My favorite example was the Charmin and Bounty Essentials execution.
When we came out of COVID, we deprioritized that part of the business simply because we
didn't have the capacity. And when we went into this period, we said we need to reignite
user growth in that part of the value segment within Family Care. The team redesigned the
proposition, adjusted the value, redesigned the packaging, and the proposition is working
extremely well, growing significant users. At the same time, we're innovating at the higher end
with the Charmin strong innovation on wider sheets, which is very intuitive and very
consumer relevant. We'll continue to do both. And I think we've made the investment over
the last nine months to get us into the right starting place. And now it's pushing forward from
here with the balanced portfolio execution and again, carefully watching value equation at each
part of our portfolio. Your next question will come from the line of Bonnie Herzog of Goldman
Sachs. Please go ahead. All right. Thank you. Good morning, everyone. I had a question on
baby care. It's encouraging to see the sequential acceleration and growth this quarter. And then
you highlighted North America and China as key drivers. So I guess against the backdrop of
increased promo intensity in the US and then disruption at one of your key competitors in
China, what has been your strategy in baby care and how sustainable do you think the
recent improvements are? Thanks. Thanks, Bonnie. Global baby care is up. Top line is growing 5%.
Shares growing 80 bits. Baby care in the US is up 3% on sales, 7% on volume, and up both in
volume share and value share. We have not yet addressed many parts of the portfolio. We have
just launched the mid-tier upgrade, which will not be the last to get to superiority.
We have not yet fixed our wipes business. And we have not yet launched the innovation
that we want to launch on swaddlers and some other parts of the premium portfolio.
We have fixed what I would call the hygiene factors, value versus growth competition.
And we are building on the trend that we see as the future growth engine for this category,
which is less babies mean more spending per baby. And that holds true in every part of the world.
And it holds true in the US. It holds true in China. And when we launch truly superior
propositions that feed into what the premium consumer is looking for,
superior dryness, softness, premium materials, safety on the highest level, ingredient safety,
we win. And that's why Amora is going to a $100 million brand in a few quarters.
And I think that will be the success model for the future. China has been doing this now
for eight quarters. The mid-tier is effectively not existent in China anymore.
And even when I take out the most recent competitive issue in China,
the business would have consistently grown in high teens and low 20s. So I do believe
that the model is very sustainable. That the strategy of being superior and trading consumers
up as we are doing on tape diapers is the same model we can apply on pants,
the same model we can apply on wipes. And I do think that is a solid growth path for the
business. And I'm excited about the innovation that's coming. And I think that does exactly
that. Your next question will come from Philippa Falorni of Citi. Please go ahead.
Hi, good morning, everyone. I wanted to ask about the US business. Andre, you mentioned
70% of top US customers holding or growing shares. That's a significant improvement,
as you called out versus last year. Where do you think it's coming mainly from? And how much
more do you have to realize in the balance of the year within your guidance? What are you
assuming in terms of improvement in share? And then in terms of the gap relative to consumption,
last year you had a lot of volatility, a lot of quarters where shipments were below consumption.
These quarters seem to have closed quite more. How should we think about that gap from an
inventory growth to net sales levels as we think about the balance of the year? Thank you.
Good morning, Philippa. Thanks for the question. I think the answer to the first question is more.
We are where we said we would be. We wanted to be at the end of the year. We want to be north
of 80%, end of the calendar year that is. And I think the North American team is working
towards that objective. The recipe doesn't change. Where we don't grow users, we very quickly go into
diagnosis mode. And we're very quickly in a combination of the customer, the customer team
on the P&G side, the category team develop an action plan. And we fund that action plan when
it cannot be funded within the category commitments. And that cycle time is only
improving. We're having these conversations in a structural way every quarter, but we're having
them at hawk almost every week. So I feel good about the urgency. I feel very good about the
clarity of being consumer-led in those conversations. Because the secret here is not to
try to buy more share. The secret here is to tailor the adjustments to superiority to the
specific needs of that retailer's shopper. Be it price points, be it claims, be it part of the
portfolio that we present at the retailer. That will continue. Again, our objective that we
stated before is 80% by the end of the calendar year. Inventory dynamics, you said it, the base
period is going to be the source of volatility here. As you know, we had a significant inventory
shift in quarter three in the US. That will impact this quarter three as well. But we'll
have to see how the flow of promotion events, how the flow of innovation evolves.
I feel confident in the semester guidance that we just gave you. 3% organic sales in the front,
a little bit more in the back half. Quarter by quarter, this might shift a little bit because
of those dynamics. But I feel confident in three and three plus front half back half.
Your next question will come from the line of Chris Carey of Wells Fargo Securities. Please go ahead.
Hi, thanks so much for the question. Andre, I just wanted to clarify that last statement and
then that I have a follow up. Just regarding the fiscal Q2 deceleration despite the easier
compare, we need to think about a roughly one point shift in Europe and then it sounds like
you're just more broadly assessing strength of consumer as we get into the end of the calendar
year. Given the higher inflation backdrop, is that really the premise of just embedding
that deceleration for now into fiscal Q2? And then just from a category perspective,
I think this is the best fabric care, pipeline growth we've seen in a few years.
Can you just give us a bit of context on category growth rates globally and perhaps some of the
market share dynamics that are underway, most specifically in the US and Europe given
some of the innovation and competitive activity you've seen in those regions? Thank you.
Thanks Chris. I think you answered your first part of the question. I think it's exactly that.
Look, gas prices are continuing to come up. Midterms and related outcomes in the Middle East
are still a source of significant volatility going into quarter two. Base period dynamics,
inventory shifts. So you put it all together, we don't want to get ahead of ourselves. We
think 3% is a healthy growth rate within this context and we know there's volatility
quarter over quarter. So we want to be realistic in assessing the strength and straight line of the
underlying momentum. The strength is real, but it won't be a straight line. Fabric care,
specifically you're right, in the US fabric care business is growing at 4%. So strong results.
In Europe we're growing 5% and we're growing share in both regions. So North America value
share is up 70 bips. Europe value share is up 60 bips over the last three months.
And those are the two largest markets in fabric care. Fabric enhancers are growing
and the laundry part of the business is growing. So it's consistent across the portfolio.
The innovation, I think the improvements we're making in delivering superiority, EVO,
the Tide Liquid Boosted innovation. We innovated on gain, both on liquid and on unit dose,
and that's driving growth. We have innovation on fabric enhancers, the Luxe Edition,
that's driving growth. So I think again the return to a consumer centric
assessment of superiority. Are we growing users? If we're not growing users, what are the right
interventions? Have led the fabric care teams both in Europe and in North America to make
the right calls and I think those calls are playing out in growth. And I feel good about
the type of growth we're generating slightly ahead of market, but every one of these
initiatives is growing the market. Given the premium of gain, the premium of Tide,
the premium of EVO, it's actually expanding the category by delighting the consumer at each value
tier more than anybody else. Your next question will come from the line of Nick Modi of RBC
Capital Markets. Please go ahead. Yeah, thank you. Good morning everyone. Andre,
maybe you can just peel back the onion on China. You know, there's been a lot of macro
volatility, you know, a lot of commentary that the macro backdrop remains poor. I think you made
the same comments, but the business is doing really well. So I just wanted to kind of understand
exactly, you know, like what's going on? Is this a beauty specific thing? You know,
